debate_title: As AI automates cognitive labor, should policy prioritize...

conflicts.point: Whether a graduated, share-keyed compute levy is enforceable, given that the cloud-provider billing ledger only observes managed cloud runs and not on-prem clusters, foreign-cloud capacity, or sharded multi-provider runs.

positions.stance: The audit chokepoint goes blind precisely where rents concentrate; frontier training can migrate off the auditable managed-cloud surface once a levy bites, making the levy's own falsification metric uncomputable.

Compute share is auditable at the cloud provider's ledger where a handful of firms already see every customer training run; the design inverts the flat-rate problem by exempting sub-threshold entrants.

conflicts.point: Whether the data-center buildout (power-purchase agreements, interconnect queue positions, fab allocations) is captured by incumbents or remains contestable by new entrants.

positions.stance: PPAs are assignable, interconnect positions transferable, and fab allocation rolls on two-to-three-year cycles; the contested resource is the next block, so the buildout is contestable rather than captured.

Once a firm signs a 15-year power contract in Iowa with grid interconnect and fab allocation booked years out, that capacity is captured and no later wage-insurance check unwinds it; the buildout is an irreversible path the cushion argument ignores.

conflicts.point: Whether a per-transition displacement charge is adequate, given it fires only on clean elimination events and never books reconfiguration harm where a worker's task is changed and wage depressed without a layoff.

positions.stance: The charge internalizes a measurable harm priced against an observable event; the ledger should also count the diagnostic that never shipped due to compliance delay.
The measurability that makes the charge defensible makes it systematically incomplete — the reconfigured paralegal never appears on the ledger because no layoff triggered the charge.

conflicts.point: Whether inaction (a do-little reversible cushion) or a structural levy is the more irreversible choice when weighed against entrenched concentration of the productivity engine.

positions.stance: A dialable statutory rate is easier to repeal than a structural transfer, but the comparison is reversible-rate versus contestable-buildout, not locked-in-buildout.

Inaction is not the reversible baseline; a repealable subsidy that locks in an unrepealable concentration is not the cautious choice, and the irreversibility test must run on both sides of the ledger.

verdicts.conflict: Whether a graduated, share-keyed compute levy is enforceable given that cloud-provider billing ledgers observe only managed cloud runs and not on-prem, foreign-cloud, or sharded multi-provider capacity.
verdicts.rationale: Both positions cite the same chokepoint — the handful of cloud providers that see customer training runs — and dispute only what share of frontier compute escapes that ledger via on-prem, colocated, foreign-cloud, or sharded capacity. Neither side supplies a measurement of the off-ledger fraction, so the enforceability question turns on an unquantified empirical magnitude. The skeptic's design includes a stated falsification condition (the levy fails if the top five firms' compute share rises over a measurable window), which adds testability, but the accelerationist's leakage channels are concrete and unrebutted on substance.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Data on what fraction of training runs above 10^25 FLOP occur on auditable managed-cloud surfaces versus on-prem, foreign-cloud, or sharded configurations, plus evidence on whether levy imposition shifts that fraction over time.

verdicts.conflict: Whether the data-center buildout (power-purchase agreements, interconnect queue positions, fab allocations) is captured by incumbents or remains contestable by new entrants.
verdicts.rationale: The capture position names a concrete, dated commitment — a 15-year Iowa power contract with booked interconnect and fab allocation — that fixes capacity on a timescale no annual cushion payment reverses. The contestability rebuttal asserts that PPAs are assignable, interconnect positions transferable, and fab allocation rolls on two-to-three-year cycles, but offers no evidence that transfer actually occurs at scale or that contested next-block capacity offsets the durations of signed contracts. The asymmetry between a 15-year lock and a 2-3 year refresh cycle favors the capture claim on the concrete numbers presented.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence on secondary-market transfer rates for PPAs and interconnect positions, and on how much frontier-relevant capacity remains uncommitted in the contestable 'next block' relative to capacity locked under multi-year contracts.

verdicts.conflict: Whether a per-transition displacement charge is adequate, given it fires only on clean elimination events and never books reconfiguration harm where a worker's task changes and wage falls without a layoff.
verdicts.rationale: The completeness objection identifies a category of harm — task reconfiguration with wage depression but no layoff — that the trigger design structurally excludes, and the accelerationist concedes the charge is 'priced against an observable event.' The accelerationist's own framing thus admits the charge captures only countable elimination events, leaving the reconfigured-worker case unaddressed. The objection accounts for a wider set of displacement mechanisms than the charge can register, while the accelerationist gains administrability at the cost of coverage.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical estimates of the share of AI-attributable wage loss that flows through clean layoffs versus task reconfiguration without separation, which would establish how much harm the charge omits.

verdicts.conflict: Whether inaction (a reversible cushion) or a structural levy is the more irreversible choice when weighed against entrenched concentration of the productivity engine.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist argues that the precautionary bar should fall hardest on capture-prone, hard-to-unwind structural transfers (C13), while the safetyist argues the irreversibility test must run on both sides of the ledger because a repealable subsidy can lock in unrepealable concentration (C18). The safetyist's C17 unbundling move — distinguishing a per-transition liability and auditable accountability regime from a standing compute levy or ownership transfer — neutralizes the accelerationist's higher-bar argument only if those instruments are genuinely separable, which the accelerationist disputes. The dispute reduces to a contested premise about whether inaction is a neutral reversible baseline, and resolution depends on the empirical buildout question (disagreement 2) rather than on the value framing alone.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Resolution of whether the data-center buildout is captured or contestable; if capture is established, the claim that inaction is the reversible baseline weakens, and if contestability is established, the structural levy's higher reversibility bar holds.

verdicts.conflict: Whether repealing the depreciation subsidy moves firm prices toward an undistorted neutral line, or whether no clean undistorted baseline exists given monopoly rents.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist's directional argument (C11) depends on the existence of a 'neutral marginal-cost line' that subtraction moves toward and a levy moves below. The skeptic (C14) identifies that the post-repeal price sits at a monopoly-rent level rather than a competitive one, removing the fixed reference point the sign-of-the-move test requires. The accelerationist's C25 rebuttal concedes 'neither lands on a clean line,' which weakens the original directional claim that relied on a defined neutral baseline.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence on the degree of market power in frontier AI and cloud markets; if prices approximate competitive marginal cost, the directional test recovers a usable baseline, restoring the accelerationist's argument.

verdicts.conflict: Whether the firm's automation incentive is already policy-distorted, undermining the claim that distribution can be left to the market.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic repurposes the accelerationist's own cited evidence — Acemoglu and Restrepo's 2020 finding that the U.S. tax code over-subsidizes capital through accelerated depreciation — to show the automation decision is pre-distorted rather than market-neutral. The accelerationist cites this finding to argue for subtracting the distortion, but does not contest that the baseline is non-neutral, which is the skeptic's load-bearing point. Because both sides accept the underlying evidence, the inference that 'the market distributing gains' is not a neutral description follows directly.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that the capital-labor tax differential is small or offset by other provisions, which would weaken the claim that the automation incentive is materially policy-distorted.
